body.text: India hosted the inaugural Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi on November 20-22. It drew representatives from 22 countries, including a federal minister from arch-rival Pakistan.
The visit by Musadik Masood Malik, Pakistan’s Minister for Environment and Climate Change, comes amid serious strains in India-Pakistan relations stemming from military clashes in May 2025.

Malik’s visit to India for the SCO event in New Delhi is the first at the ministerial level from Pakistan since May 2023, when then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended the SCO Council of Foreign Ministers’ meeting that India hosted in Goa. It has raised questions about a possible thaw between the two South Asian nations.

Ties have been particularly strained since the 2025 military clashes that followed a terrorist attack on tourists in Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed the attack on a group that it said was a proxy for Pakistan-based terrorist organization Lashkar-e-Taiba, known to target Indian interests.

India-Pakistan relations began unravelling well before that, though, in 2016. After two major terrorist attacks – the first on an Indian Air Force base in Pathankot in Punjab and the other on an Indian Army camp in Uri in Kashmir—India carried out a cross-border military raid to take out terrorist training camps inside Pakistan-controlled territory. The move was part of a changed strategy under which India said it would take military action to eliminate terrorist camps on Pakistan-controlled territory. India not only stopped engaging Pakistan at the bilateral level as a result but also called off attendance at the multilateral South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) meet that Pakistan was scheduled to host. SAARC has been dormant since then.

In 2019, India cut off trade ties with Pakistan after a terrorist attack on a bus carrying Indian paramilitary men at Pulwama in Kashmir. The Indian Air Force struck terrorist training camps inside Pakistan in retaliation. Tensions worsened again that year when Pakistan expelled India’s high commissioner and recalled its envoy from New Delhi after India revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s autonomy in August. New Delhi split the state into two union territories, bringing both under its direct rule.
In an address to the nation after the Pahalgam attack last year, Modi outlined the contours of India’s Pakistan policy.

“India’s stand is very clear… Terror and talks cannot go together… Terror and trade cannot go together…. Water and blood cannot flow together,” Modi said. A terrorist attack against India would not go unpunished and New Delhi would strike Pakistan territory. India would also not hold back from taking action for fear of triggering a nuclear conflict, he said.
Against this backdrop, India’s invitation to Pakistan to attend the SCO meet has drawn criticism from opposition parties, with some calling India’s Pakistan policy “confused.”

During his time in India, Malik visited the Taj Mahal in Agra and other monuments in New Delhi. Images of Malik seated in the front row, although not alongside Modi but several seats apart, and another of India’s Minister of Culture Gajendra Singh Shekhawat engaging Malik in a conversation at lunch have also been slammed by the opposition.

The SCO has been one of the rare forums where India and Pakistan have been seated at the same table together since ties started fraying a decade ago. Both India and Pakistan officially joined the SCO as full members in 2017.

After Zardari’s 2023 visit to India, India’s Minister for External Affairs S Jaishankar traveled to Pakistan in 2024. India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh has also attended SCO meetings — in Moscow in 2020 and in Tajikistan last month.

On none of these occasions was bilateral ties in focus. That was also true in the case of Malik’s current visit to India. “This [SCO Forum] is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan,” External Affairs Ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X.

With the emphasis clearly being on the multilateral, expecting a thaw on the bilateral would be premature. Still, that hasn’t quelled speculation. Fueling it was Malik’s rather restrained comments on relations with India.
At international forums, including SCO meetings, India and Pakistan routinely spar over the Kashmir dispute and India often seeks to isolate Pakistan on its alleged support for anti-India terrorism.

At the recent SCO event in Delhi, Malik’s comments were largely restricted to issues at hand – culture and civilizational dialogue – even in the face of provocative questions by Indian journalists on terrorism, the Kashmir dispute, and bilateral relations. Malik even seemed to concur with a point Modi made, calling for dialogue among civilizations. Interestingly, Malik’s comments were included in a statement put out by the Indian government on November 21.

What makes Malik’s temperance intriguing is the fact that in June this year, he was quoted as saying that Pakistan would “cut off those hands” that are attempting to control the Indus waters. This follows India’s decision in April 2025 to place the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance following the Pahalgam attack. The pact divides the river Indus and its tributaries between India and Pakistan. India consumes waters of three eastern rivers – Sutlej, Beas and Ravi – while Pakistan uses waters of three western rivers – Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab.
When asked about his remarks during his India visit, Malik said his current visit was only in the context of the SCO, and he would discuss the Indus Waters Treaty when formally invited to do so.

“I think the invitation to Pakistan for the SCO meet is a positive thing,” former Indian High Commissioner to Pakistan T.C.A Raghavan told The Diplomat. Pointing out that Pakistan was chairing the SCO this year, Raghavan said this could “explain Malik’s restraint.” Malik “thinks there is little to be gained by being controversial on this particular platform,” he said.
“Whether Malik’s restraint means anything more than that, I don’t think so,” Raghavan said when asked whether it could lead to an unfreeze in ties.

As SCO chair, Pakistan will host a slew of meetings next year, with invitations expected to be extended to Jaishankar, Singh, and India’s National Security Advisor Ajit Doval. Modi is also set to be invited to the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting. If bilateral relations remain testy, a Modi visit would be unlikely.
